title: New HTML, old stylesheet
question: After a deploy, some users see the new page layout with the old stylesheet — broken buttons, overlapping text — for up to an hour. How should the assets be cached?
context: HTML, CSS and JavaScript are all served through a CDN with a one-hour cache lifetime. Files keep the same names between releases, such as /app.css.

options.label: Purge the whole CDN cache as the last step of every deploy
options.why: It narrows the window rather than closing it: browsers keep their own copy of /app.css, purges take time to reach every edge, and every deploy sends a burst of misses to the origin. The names still do not say which version a file is.

options.label: Lower the cache lifetime on everything to one minute
options.why: The mismatch still happens, for a minute instead of an hour, and the CDN now fetches everything from the origin sixty times as often. Short lifetimes trade correctness for cost without guaranteeing either.

options.label: Hash each file's content into its name; cache HTML only briefly
options.why: A new stylesheet gets a new name, so it can never be confused with the old one and can be cached for a year. Only the HTML, which names the assets it needs, has to be fresh — and it is small. Old and new versions coexist safely during the rollout.

options.label: Stop caching CSS and JavaScript at the CDN and serve them live
options.why: It removes the mismatch at the CDN by removing the CDN's benefit for the heaviest files, and browser caches still hold the old /app.css. Every page view now pays for the origin round trip.
